subtopic_detail: ripening an unfavourable cervix at term in a woman with one previous caesarean who wants a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit seeing a 32 year old woman at 41 weeks and 0 days in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was born by lower segment caesarean section for a breech presentation at term, with no infection and an uncomplicated recovery.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the foetus is cephalic with an estimated weight on the fiftieth centile, and the placenta is fundal and well clear of the previous scar. She has had no contractions and her membranes are intact. She is clear that she would like to give birth vaginally and has attended two counselling appointments about her options. On vaginal examination the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm, posterior and the station is minus three, giving a Bishop score of 3. The cardiotocograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 138
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, Bishop score 3, membranes intact, no uterine tenderness or scar tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 138, good variability and accelerations, amniotic fluid index within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate method of induction of labour?

options.text: Transcervical balloon catheter for ripening, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Mechanical ripening with a balloon catheter avoids the excess uterine rupture risk associated with prostaglandin ripening in a scarred uterus while still converting an unfavourable cervix, and it is the preferred method in Australian practice for this situation. Continuous electronic foetal monitoring follows once labour is established because an abnormal foetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar dehiscence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Vaginal prostaglandin E2 gel repeated after six hours, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Prostaglandin ripening roughly doubles the risk of uterine rupture compared with spontaneous labour in a woman with a previous caesarean, and that risk is the reason mechanical methods are preferred. The two approaches achieve similar cervical change, so the difference is entirely one of scar safety. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Vaginal misoprostol in low dose repeated six hourly, then amniotomy and oxytocin
options.rationale: Misoprostol carries the highest rupture risk of all ripening agents in a scarred uterus and is contraindicated for induction at term after a previous caesarean. Its use in obstetrics at term is confined to women with no uterine scar. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics

options.text: Amniotomy today followed by an oxytocin infusion titrated to contraction frequency
options.rationale: Artificial rupture of membranes is not feasible with a closed, firm, posterior cervix at station minus three, and oxytocin without cervical ripening in this setting produces a prolonged induction with a high failure rate. The unfavourable Bishop score is what makes a ripening step necessary first. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Elective repeat caesarean section arranged for tomorrow given her unfavourable cervix
options.rationale: A repeat caesarean is a legitimate choice and must remain available to her, but an unfavourable cervix alone is not a contraindication to induction, and abandoning her stated preference without offering a safe ripening method is not supported. This would be the answer if she changed her mind or if a contraindication to labour emerged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Around three quarters of women who labour after one previous lower segment caesarean achieve a vaginal birth, and the background risk of uterine rupture in spontaneous labour is roughly one in two hundred. That risk rises with induction and augmentation, and the rise is steepest with prostaglandin agents, which is why mechanical ripening has become the preferred approach when the cervix is unfavourable. Contraindications to attempting vaginal birth include a previous classical or inverted T incision, previous uterine rupture, a placenta praevia or accreta, and any other standard indication for caesarean. The practical requirements for a trial of labour are a hospital with immediate access to theatre and blood, continuous electronic foetal monitoring in established labour, and intravenous access. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign of scar rupture and precedes scar pain, loss of contractions, vaginal bleeding and maternal haemodynamic change.
key_points: Uterine rupture risk in spontaneous labour after one caesarean is about one in two hundred
Prostaglandin ripening approximately doubles that risk and misoprostol is contraindicated
Mechanical balloon ripening is preferred for an unfavourable cervix
Continuous electronic foetal monitoring is required in established labour
An abnormal foetal heart rate pattern is the earliest sign of scar rupture
explanation.pearls: Two or more previous caesareans, a short interdelivery interval of under eighteen months, and induction of labour each independently raise rupture risk, and it is the combination rather than any single factor that most often tips counselling toward a repeat caesarean.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: what to do with a treated hypothyroid woman's replacement dose on the day she reports a positive pregnancy test
stem:
You are the general practitioner taking a telephone call from a 30 year old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was five weeks ago and the pregnancy was planned.

She has autoimmune hypothyroidism diagnosed six years ago with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily without missing doses. Her thyroid function was checked three months ago as part of her preconception care and her thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.0 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine. She takes no other medication, no iron and no calcium supplement, and takes her tablet on an empty stomach each morning. She has no goitre, no palpitations and no heat intolerance. She asks whether she should change anything now or wait until her first antenatal appointment in three weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and free thyroxine within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her today?

options.text: Continue the same daily dose and have thyroid function checked at twelve weeks
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone requirement rises from very early in the first trimester, so holding the dose steady for seven weeks leaves her underdosed during the period when foetal brain development depends entirely on maternal hormone. A pre pregnancy level of 2.0 does not provide a margin large enough to absorb that rise. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Take two extra tablets each week from today and check thyroid function in four weeks
options.rationale: Requirement increases by roughly a quarter to a third within the first weeks, and adding two extra tablets each week delivers about that increase immediately using the tablets she already has. Rechecking in four weeks then confirms the first trimester target has been reached rather than assumed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Arrange thyroid function testing today and adjust the dose once the result arrives
options.rationale: Testing is certainly needed, but waiting several days for the result before acting delays an increase that is predictable in every treated hypothyroid pregnancy, so the dose is raised at the same time the test is ordered. This is one of the few situations where empirical dose adjustment precedes the result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Reduce the daily dose slightly to allow for the pregnancy related rise in hormone
options.rationale: The transient fall in thyroid stimulating hormone seen in early pregnancy reflects stimulation of the thyroid by human chorionic gonadotropin in women with a functioning gland, which she does not have. In treated hypothyroidism the requirement rises rather than falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Add liothyronine to her current regimen and check thyroid function in four weeks
options.rationale: Combination therapy with triiodothyronine is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta poorly and suppresses maternal thyroid stimulating hormone without supplying the thyroxine the foetus needs. Levothyroxine alone is the only appropriate replacement in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Maternal thyroxine requirement rises early in pregnancy because oestrogen driven thyroxine binding globulin increases, human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the gland, placental deiodinase increases hormone degradation, and the plasma volume expands. Women with an intact gland accommodate this automatically, whereas women on replacement cannot and need their dose increased. The foetal thyroid does not begin producing hormone until around twelve weeks, so the whole of early neurodevelopment depends on transplacental maternal thyroxine, which is why the increase is made immediately rather than at the first antenatal visit. The recommended first trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L, and levels are rechecked every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy and at least once thereafter. Iron, calcium and antacids, all common in pregnancy, bind levothyroxine in the gut and must be separated from it by at least four hours, which is a frequent and easily missed cause of apparent dose failure.
key_points: Requirement rises by roughly 25 to 30 per cent in the first trimester
Two extra tablets per week delivers approximately that increase without a new prescription
First trimester target is a thyroid stimulating hormone below 2.5 mIU/L
The foetal thyroid does not function until about twelve weeks
Iron and calcium must be taken at least four hours apart from levothyroxine
explanation.pearls: Recheck thyroid function four weeks after any dose change and then every four to six weeks until mid pregnancy, and return to the pre pregnancy dose immediately after birth with a further check six weeks postpartum.

subtopic_detail: a seizure free woman on valproate who wants to conceive within the year, and whether folate supplementation is sufficient mitigation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old teacher who tells you she and her partner would like to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that began at fourteen.

She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for six years and has been free of seizures for the past three. She holds an unrestricted driver licence. She currently uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception. She has not seen her neurologist for two years because she has been well. She has no other medical conditions, takes no other medication, and there is no family history of neural tube defect. She asks whether she should simply start folic acid and continue as she is.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, blood pressure 112/70, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and add folic acid 5 mg daily now
options.rationale: High dose folate is recommended for any woman with epilepsy planning pregnancy, but it does not offset the dose dependent risk of neural tube defects, other major malformations and impaired childhood neurodevelopment that valproate carries. Adding folate without changing the drug gives the appearance of mitigation without the substance of it. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.text: Continue valproate and arrange an early detailed morphology scan once she conceives
options.rationale: Detailed anomaly imaging will detect structural defects but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental and autism spectrum outcomes that constitute the largest part of the harm, and by then the exposure has already occurred. Surveillance is not a substitute for avoiding the exposure. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer urgently to neurology to plan a change of medication before she conceives
options.rationale: A supervised switch to an agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam must be completed and stability confirmed before conception, because changing during an established pregnancy exposes the foetus to both drugs and risks breakthrough seizures. Referring now, while she still has effective contraception in place, is what creates the time the switch requires. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory

options.text: Stop the valproate now and review her seizure control again in three months
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic clonic seizures risks status epilepticus, loss of her driver licence and injury, and maternal seizures in pregnancy carry their own foetal risks including hypoxia and trauma. Any change is a supervised cross titration rather than a cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Change her today to carbamazepine at an equivalent dose and review in one month
options.rationale: Switching an antiseizure medication in a woman with generalised epilepsy is specialist work, and carbamazepine can aggravate generalised seizure types including absence and myoclonic seizures as well as carrying its own teratogenic risk. The specific hazard here is choosing an agent that is wrong for her seizure syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiseizure medications, with major congenital malformations in roughly one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment, reduced cognitive scores and increased autism spectrum diagnoses in a substantially larger proportion. Both risks are dose dependent, and there is no dose that has been shown to be free of neurodevelopmental effect. Australian regulatory advice requires that valproate is not used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, that effective contraception is in place, and that the risks are discussed and documented at least annually. Preconception is the only safe point at which to change treatment, because a switch made after a positive pregnancy test exposes the foetus during organogenesis to both the old and the new drug. Where valproate genuinely cannot be replaced, the dose is minimised, the daily dose is divided, high dose folate is given, and the pregnancy is managed jointly by neurology and obstetrics.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformations in about ten per cent and neurodevelopmental harm in more
Both effects are dose dependent and folate does not offset them
Any switch is completed and stability confirmed before conception
Contraception is maintained until the new regimen is established
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and loss of driving privileges
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises substantially through pregnancy because of oestrogen induced glucuronidation, so levels fall and doses often need increasing, then must be reduced promptly within days of birth to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Safety Advisory
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: epigastric pain with falling platelets and rising transaminases at thirty four weeks when the blood pressure is only mildly raised
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 34 year old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her first pregnancy who came in overnight with twelve hours of pain under her ribs on the right and persistent nausea. She thought she had eaten something that disagreed with her.

She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no ankle swelling that she has noticed. Her blood pressure at her last antenatal visit a week ago was 118 over 72 with no proteinuria. She has vomited twice. Her blood glucose is normal and she is not confused or drowsy. Foetal movements have been normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She takes no regular medication and has had no previous liver or gallbladder problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 148/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Tender in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium, no guarding, reflexes normal with no clonus, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400), alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase 720 U/L (120 to 250), haptoglobin low, blood film shows fragmented red cells, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), international normalised ratio 1.0, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, urine protein creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (less than 30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat the full blood count before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: Platelets are consumed rapidly in this process so a transfusion given without delivering produces only a transient rise, and it is reserved for active bleeding or for cover immediately before an operative procedure. Transfusing to defer the decision treats the number rather than the disease. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Australia

options.text: Manage expectantly with twice weekly bloods and birth planned at 37 weeks
options.rationale: Expectant management is considered only before 34 weeks and only where maternal and foetal parameters are stable, whereas she is past 34 weeks with an actively deteriorating haematological and hepatic picture. The syndrome characteristically progresses over hours rather than days. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Give dexamethasone to raise the platelet count and continue the pregnancy further
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do produce a transient improvement in platelet count but have not been shown to improve maternal or perinatal outcome, and using them to justify prolonging the pregnancy is the error rather than the drug itself. Antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity are a separate and legitimate indication. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy, and plan birth today
options.rationale: Haemolysis with fragmented cells, transaminases above twice the upper limit and platelets below 100 x10^9/L at 34 weeks establishes a severe manifestation of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in which the only definitive treatment is birth. Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and the blood pressure treated while delivery is organised. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Start oral labetalol and arrange outpatient review with repeat bloods in two days
options.rationale: Lowering the blood pressure prevents maternal stroke but does nothing to halt the underlying endothelial and hepatic process, so treating the pressure alone and sending her home would allow the syndrome to progress unobserved. Her pressure is also not in the severe range, which is precisely why it cannot be used to gauge severity here. (Source: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets constitute a severe variant of pre-eclampsia that can present with only modest hypertension and minimal proteinuria, so severity is judged on the end organ picture rather than on the blood pressure reading. Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain from hepatic capsular distension is the characteristic symptom and is often misattributed to reflux, gallbladder disease or gastroenteritis, which delays diagnosis. The main differential is acute fatty liver of pregnancy, which is distinguished by hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with a prolonged international normalised ratio, a rising creatinine and often encephalopathy, none of which is present here. Complications include eclampsia, placental abruption, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and hepatic haematoma or rupture, and the disease may worsen for the first twenty four to forty eight hours after birth, so postnatal surveillance continues. Birth is the only definitive treatment, and the decision to deliver is made on the maternal condition rather than on the gestation once past thirty four weeks.
key_points: Blood pressure may be only mildly raised and proteinuria minimal
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain reflects hepatic capsular stretch
Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and rising creatinine suggest acute fatty liver instead
Birth is the only definitive treatment and is not deferred past 34 weeks
The disease can worsen in the first two days after birth
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis and continued for twenty four hours after birth, with monitoring of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output, and calcium gluconate kept immediately available as the antidote for toxicity.

sources.label: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: first trimester anticoagulation for a mechanical mitral prosthesis where the daily warfarin requirement sits at the embryopathy dose threshold
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 31 year old woman who had a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement at twenty four for rheumatic heart disease. She had a positive pregnancy test three days ago and is now six weeks by her dates.

She takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 2.5 to 3.5 and her results have been within range at every check for two years. She has had no thromboembolic event and no bleeding. Her echocardiogram four months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no pannus, no regurgitation and a normal left atrial size, and she is in sinus rhythm. She has no other medical conditions and takes no other medication. She has read online that warfarin harms babies and has already missed two doses because she was frightened to take it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 and regular, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, chest clear, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 1.6 today, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, transthoracic echocardiogram four months ago showed normal prosthetic function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant for the first trimester, then resume warfarin
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves at any time because a randomised trial in non pregnant patients was stopped early for excess valve thrombosis and stroke, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. This is the one option that is wrong on both counts simultaneously. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation until twelve weeks, then restart warfarin at her usual dose
options.rationale: Pregnancy is a strongly prothrombotic state and a mechanical mitral prosthesis left unanticoagulated for six weeks carries a high risk of valve thrombosis, which is frequently fatal to both mother and foetus. Her missed doses and an international normalised ratio already down at 1.6 make this the immediate danger rather than a theoretical one. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to twice daily therapeutic enoxaparin with dosing guided by her weight alone
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin is a legitimate first trimester strategy and the one chosen when the warfarin requirement is high, but it must be given twice daily with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment, because valve thrombosis has occurred in pregnant women dosed on weight without monitoring. The flaw is the omission of monitoring rather than the choice of drug. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion for the whole first trimester
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin carries the highest rate of valve thrombosis of all the regimens used in this setting and commits her to hospital or to an indwelling line for six weeks with attendant infection and osteoporosis risk. Its proper place is the immediate peripartum window, not the first trimester. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Restore warfarin at her usual dose now with close monitoring after documented counselling
options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose dependent and is low when the daily requirement is 5 mg or less, so continuing warfarin through the first trimester carries the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis and an acceptable foetal risk at her dose of 4 mg. Her subtherapeutic ratio of 1.6 makes restoration urgent, and the decision is made with her after explicit counselling because both branches carry real risk. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with a mechanical heart valve is one of the highest risk cardiac situations in obstetrics, and no anticoagulation strategy is free of harm, so the task is to choose the least bad option for the individual woman and to document the discussion. Warfarin gives the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between six and twelve weeks, together with foetal intracranial haemorrhage later in pregnancy. That embryopathy risk is dose dependent, and the widely used threshold is a daily requirement of 5 mg or less, below which continuation through the first trimester is considered reasonable and above which a switch to low molecular weight heparin between six and twelve weeks is preferred. Heparins do not cross the placenta and so carry no foetal risk, but they protect the valve less reliably and demand twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment. Mitral position, older generation prostheses, atrial fibrillation and a previous thromboembolic event all raise thrombotic risk and push the balance back toward warfarin.
key_points: No regimen is risk free; the choice is documented shared decision making
Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent, with 5 mg daily as the usual threshold
The vulnerable window for embryopathy is six to twelve weeks
Low molecular weight heparin requires twice daily dosing with peak anti factor Xa monitoring
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve
explanation.pearls: Warfarin is converted to intravenous unfractionated heparin at around thirty six weeks and the heparin stopped four to six hours before birth, because a warfarinised foetus has an anticoagulated brain and vaginal birth then carries an unacceptable risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
